summary: Defines a human-readable text string form of an X.500 distinguished name, for cases like mail messages where a name has to travel outside a directory protocol. It was a standards-track specification. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1779, RFC 3494.

plainLanguage.summary: A formal name in a big directory is like a long file path. This memo says how to write that path as plain text so people can put it in an email.

subtitle: A readable text format for writing down an X.500 directory name, such as on a business card or in an email.

tldr.problem: X.500 distinguished names are encoded in ASN.1, which is no use when a name must be written in a mail message or on a business card.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a string notation of comma or semicolon separated key=value components such as CN=..., OU=..., O=..., C=..., with quoting and a hexadecimal escape so that any distinguished name can be written.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Historic and was replaced by RFC 1779 and RFC 3494.

facts.label: Required keywords
facts.value: CN, L, ST, O, OU, C

today: RFC 1485 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1779 and RFC 3494, so it should be read only as an early specification of the format.

sections.title: Why a Notation Is Needed
sections.content:
The OSI Directory, commonly known as X.500, uses distinguished names (DNs) as the primary keys to its entries. They are encoded in ASN.1, so people cannot easily pass them around. When a name has to travel between users who are not using a directory protocol, for example on a business card or in an email message, a string form that is user oriented is needed.

This notation targets general, user-oriented use, and in particular the names of humans. The memo notes that other syntaxes may suit other uses; the OSF syntax, which uses "/" as a separator and resembles UNIX filenames, may suit some system-oriented uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer's way of writing a name is a secret code. People need a version they can read out loud and write in a letter.

sections.title: Goals and Informal Definition
sections.content:
The goals are an unambiguous representation, an intuitive format for most names, full generality (any distinguished name can be represented), flexibility of layout, and a clear view of what the name contains.

A name is written as components separated by a comma, with the least significant component first. For example CN=Christian Huitema, O=INRIA, C=FR. A semicolon may be used instead of a comma, and a name may be folded over several lines. In running text the whole name is delimited with < and >. A multi-valued Relative Distinguished Name is written with +, as in OU=Sales + CN=J. Smith, O=Widget Inc., C=US.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the person's name first, then their department, then their company, then their country, like an address that gets bigger and bigger.

sections.title: Formal Definition, Quoting and Keywords
sections.content:
A BNF grammar based on the one in RFC 822 defines the format. It is written over an abstract character set. Quoting with double quotes is used for strings containing characters such as a comma, a plus sign, an equals sign, a quote mark, angle brackets, a hash sign or a semicolon, for strings with leading or trailing spaces, and for strings with consecutive spaces. An example is O="Sue, Grabbit and Runn".

For pathological cases there is an escape mechanism: attribute types may be written in dotted form (for example OID.2.6.53) and attribute values in hexadecimal (for example #0A56CF).

The grammar makes the attribute keyword optional, but this specification makes it mandatory. Implementations must support six keywords, and the IANA maintains a register of valid keywords. Only string-type attributes are considered, and the interface is assumed to translate the string into PrintableString or T.61. In a multi-component RDN the types must be explicit.
sections.plainLanguage: If a name has a comma in it, you put it inside quote marks so nobody thinks it is the end of a part. For very strange names there is a secret-code mode written in numbers.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC lists several complete names. One is CN=Marshall T. Rose, O=Dover Beach Consulting, L=Santa Clara, ST=California, C=US. Another is CN=FTAM Service, CN=Bells, OU=Computer Science, O=University College London, C=GB, which shows a service entry deep in an organisation. The author's own entry appears as CN=Steve Hardcastle-Kille, OU=Computer Science, O=University College London, C=GB.

In its informal section the memo also shows a name where a locality is used, CN=James Hacker, L=Basingstoke, O=Widget Inc, CN=GB, to illustrate how different attribute types are handled.

The memo says security issues are not discussed. It also notes that RFC 1484 uses the same notation and relaxes some of its constraints for friendlier input; see RFC 1484.
sections.plainLanguage: It shows a handful of real-looking addresses so you can see the pattern: name, department, company, country.
